summary.text: A Plinian eruption is a volcanic eruption like the 79 AD eruption of Mount Vesuvius, which destroyed the Roman cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum.
Powerful, continuous gas-driven blasts throw out large amounts of pumice and send columns of debris and hot gas high into the stratosphere.
So much magma can be ejected that the chamber below empties and the top of the volcano collapses into a caldera.

facts.label: Described by
facts.value: Pliny the Younger, in a letter

facts.label: Usual lava
facts.value: Dacitic or rhyolitic, rich in silica

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: Under a day to days or months

facts.label: Ultra-Plinian threshold
facts.value: Column 45 km high, or 41 km more recently

items.prompt: Photos of a huge eruption column show lightning bolts flashing inside the ash. What causes them?

options.label: Storm clouds that happen to drift overhead
Hot lava sparking as it touches the air
Electric charge built up around the rising ash
Magnetic pulses coming from the Earth's core

items.explain: Charges accumulate in the air around the rising ash column and their sudden discharge often causes lightning.

items.prompt: After a Plinian eruption, the volcano's summit has been replaced by a huge basin. Why?

options.label: The drained magma chamber let the top fall in
Lava slowly melted the summit rock away
Rain washed off the loose ash on the peak
Glaciers carved out the summit afterward

items.explain: Ejecting so much magma can empty the chamber below, and the top of the volcano collapses to form a caldera.

items.prompt: Which kind of magma typically feeds a Plinian eruption?

options.label: Runny, low-silica basalt
Sticky, silica-rich rhyolite
Magma mixed with seawater
Magma with no gas inside

items.explain: Plinian lava is usually dacitic or rhyolitic and rich in silica; low-silica basalt rarely produces them.

items.prompt: How high can the column from a Plinian eruption climb?

options.label: A few hundred metres up
Just above the crater rim
Into outer space
Into the stratosphere

items.explain: Plinian eruptions eject columns of debris and hot gas high into the stratosphere, the second layer of the atmosphere.

items.prompt: The Hatepe eruption was labelled ultra-Plinian partly because its ash spread so widely. What did later evidence suggest?

options.label: The ash came from a different volcano
A shift in the wind spread the ash
Its column was even higher than thought
The deposit was lava, not ash at all

items.explain: Recent evidence suggests its ultra-Plinian label reflects an unrecognized shift in the wind field rather than extreme eruptive vigor.

items.prompt: Far from a Plinian eruption, people find their fields coated in a grey layer. What is it most likely to be?

options.label: Hardened lava from the flows
Salt carried up from the sea
Fine ash and powdered pumice
Large chunks of volcanic rock

items.explain: Fine ash and pulverized pumice from Plinian eruptions can be deposited over large areas.
